doc.title: Bill Kirchner interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2021

title: Why a nonet: origins and instrumentation
summary: The nonet grew from a ten-piece band he and Sam DeAngelo formed in Youngstown in summer 1974, and he reworked its book for six horns and three rhythm.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played what: early band size and instrumentation

blocks.x: Okay. When you put your nonet together, was there a consideration, perhaps you’re thinking to yourself how many wind instruments do I need to do the kinds of voicings that I want to do, and then from a practical sense balance it with the idea that it’s going to be hard to get nine people, ten, twelve people together consistently.
Okay so your question is what specifically?
How did you arrive at nine?

Well Sam DeAngelo and I had done a band of that size when we were in Youngstown, we did, I used to go back home during the summer to work in factories and whatever, making some money for college. And also, so the summer of 1974 which was just before my senior year in college we decided to put this band together which was basically a nonet plus a vibes player, it was ten pieces. So we came up with a similar instrumentation. It was trumpet, French horn, valve trombone, three reeds, one of whom was Ralph LaLama by the way, he was in college at the time at Youngstown State University, that’s where I first met him; and another was Harold Danko’s older brother Joe playing baritone. So anyway we did a few park concerts, you know, Music Performance Trust Fund concerts, so we did a couple of those and so I had that book. So when I came to New York I had that book and I decided to get together a rehearsal and just play some of those charts. So I rewrote a few of the charts with slightly different instrumentation done, so it ended up being two trumpets, doubling flugelhorns, bass trombone, three reeds with a lot of doubles, and three rhythm. And just — six horns for me was a good size. It gave you enough horns to basically duplicate just about any voicing you wanted to do, and also with having two trumpets, having the second trumpet underneath the lead trumpet makes a big difference with writing ensemble tuttis, it gives a lot of additional support that you don’t have when you only have one trumpet. So that ended up being my instrumentation of choice. And also, you know I mean it was the best of all possible worlds for me. It was — you could have enough fire power to come up

with like a big band punch if you wanted it, but at the same time it gave you the advantage of being a hip small group when you wanted that as well. And there were a lot of different colors with all the doubles and everything. That was really important, having all those doubles.
